FORM 5500 LATE FILING CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Missed the Form 5500 deadline? See what it costs to fix it.

Enter the plan year end and the date you plan to file. You get the due date (with the Form 5558 extension and weekend or holiday rollover), days late, and a side-by-side of the DOL DFVC programme cost against IRS and DOL penalty exposure, plus the steps to file.

Everything runs in this browser tab and nothing is sent anywhere. Independent of the IRS, the DOL and every plan provider. The penalty figures are from memory of the published programme and statute figures, are editable below and change over time: verify them against current DOL and IRS guidance before relying on any output.

1. Your plan

Fill in the plan, then click Calculate. If the filing date is blank, today is used.

Result

Side by side

RouteAmountWhat it is

By plan year

Plan year endDueDays lateDFVCIRS (up to)DOL (up to)

Steps to file

    2. The figures (editable)

    Written from memory of the published DFVC programme and the statute, not read from a live source. The DOL maximum is inflation-adjusted every year, so the number here may be out of date. Change any value and click Calculate again.

    The model, and what it leaves out

    • Due date is the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends. Form 5558, filed by that date, extends it to the 15th of the tenth month. A date on a Saturday, Sunday or federal holiday moves to the next business day. A holiday on a Saturday is not moved to Friday.
    • Days late are calendar days from the due date to the date you intend to file.
    • DFVC is the per-day amount, capped per report, then capped per plan across all reports. Earlier unfiled years use their own normal due dates and no extension.
    • IRS and DOL figures are statutory ceilings: the IRS per-day amount to its maximum per return, and the DOL per-day maximum with no overall cap. They are not predictions that any agency would assess them, and nothing here estimates that chance. Both are often reduced or waived on reasonable cause.
    • Savings from DFVC are the exposure minus the DFVC cost. DFVC resolves DOL civil penalties; IRS penalties are separate, so the combined figure assumes no relief of any kind.
    • Not checked: whether you already received an IRS or DOL notice (which can close the programme), late audit reports, late-filed Form 5558, the 80-120 participant rule, the exact participant and asset counts, state rules, and whether a plan is even covered by ERISA.

    Common questions

    When is Form 5500 due?

    The Form 5500 series is due on the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends: July 31 for a calendar-year plan. If that day is a Saturday, Sunday or federal holiday it moves to the next business day. Filing Form 5558 by the original due date extends it by two and a half months, to October 15 for a calendar-year plan.

    What happens if I miss the Form 5500 deadline?

    Two agencies can assess penalties: the IRS up to $250 a day to a maximum of $150,000 per return, and the DOL a civil penalty with a much higher per-day statutory maximum that is adjusted for inflation each year. Neither is automatic, but the exposure is real, and the DOL's Delinquent Filer Voluntary Compliance (DFVC) programme exists to let a filer pay a small fixed amount instead.

    How much does the DFVC programme cost?

    As published, $10 a day with a cap of $750 per late annual report and $1,500 per plan for a small plan (fewer than 100 participants), and $2,000 per report and $4,000 per plan for a large plan. These are the figures this page starts with; they are editable, and you should verify them against current DOL guidance.

    Does the DFVC programme remove IRS penalties?

    Not by itself. DFVC resolves DOL civil penalties for the reports it covers; the IRS assesses its own late-filing penalty separately, and often abates it for reasonable cause. The combined saving on this page assumes no relief of any kind, so it is a ceiling and not a forecast.

    Does a one-participant plan have to file?

    A one-participant plan files Form 5500-EZ only when its assets are more than $250,000 at the end of the plan year (or it is in its final year). At or under that, no return is due for that year. Check current IRS instructions for the threshold and the final-year rule.

    What do I file and where?

    Small plans usually file the short Form 5500-SF and large plans the full Form 5500 with schedules, both electronically through EFAST2, which needs a filing credential. A DFVC filing is made through EFAST2 with the programme's online penalty payment. A one-participant plan can file Form 5500-EZ on paper with the IRS or use the electronic 5500-SF.

    Is this tax or legal advice?

    No. It is arithmetic on the dates and rates in the editable list, with no estimate of whether any agency would assess a penalty. Confirm with the plan's adviser or the agency guidance before filing or paying anything.

    When is Form 5500 due, and what if you missed it?

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, retirement-plan, ERISA, compliance, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or the agencies' own guidance. Results depend entirely on the figures you enter. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including the penalty figures, which may be out of date.

    Not affiliated with the IRS, the DOL or any plan provider. Form 5500, EFAST2 and DFVC are names used by the agencies. This tool is independent and is not sponsored, endorsed or connected to the Internal Revenue Service, the U.S. Department of Labor, or any recordkeeper or plan administrator.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

    Everything runs in your browser. Your figures are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (plan_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

    Related tools: the solo 401(k) contribution calculator for the plan itself, the payroll tax deposit penalty calculator for another late-filing penalty, and the employee cost calculator for what a plan adds to payroll.

    Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

RETIREMENT PLANS

When is Form 5500 due, and what if you missed it?

Most small-business 401(k) sponsors learn about Form 5500 once, when a provider mentions it, and then it lands on the same July date every year. Miss it and the cost depends less on how late you are than on which route you take to fix it.

Open the free Form 5500 late filing calculator

The due date

The annual return is due on the last day of the seventh month after the plan year ends. For a calendar-year plan that is July 31. If the date falls on a Saturday, Sunday or federal holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Plan year endsNormal due dateWith Form 5558
December 31July 31October 15
June 30January 31April 15
September 30April 30July 15

Before any weekend or holiday move. Verify the dates for your plan against the current form instructions.

The extension

Filing Form 5558 by the original due date adds two and a half months, to the 15th of the tenth month after the plan year ends. It has to be filed on time to count, and it does not extend the date for anything else.

Who has to file at all

Small and large plans file every year. A one-participant plan (an owner, or an owner and spouse, and no other employees) files Form 5500-EZ only when assets exceed $250,000 at the end of the plan year, and also in the year the plan is wound up. That threshold is an editable figure in the calculator.

What a late filing can cost

Three numbers matter, and they come from different places:

RouteFigure as published
DOL DFVC programme, small plan$10 a day, up to $750 per late annual report and $1,500 per plan
DOL DFVC programme, large plan$10 a day, up to $2,000 per report and $4,000 per plan
IRS late-filing penalty$250 a day, up to $150,000 per return
DOL civil penaltya statutory maximum per day, adjusted for inflation each year, with no overall cap

Written from memory of the programme and statute and subject to change. The IRS and DOL figures are ceilings, not what is normally assessed.

The DFVC programme is the reason a late filing does not have to be frightening: a fixed, capped amount in exchange for filing before the DOL writes to you. It resolves the DOL penalty only. The IRS assesses its own penalty separately, and often abates it when there is a reasonable explanation.

What to do next

Gather the year-end assets and participant counts, prepare the right form for each late year, get an EFAST2 credential if you do not have one, and file electronically. Do not wait for a notice: the programme is for filers who have not yet had one.

The Form 5500 late filing calculator does the date arithmetic, including the extension, rollover and multiple unfiled years, and puts the DFVC cost next to the IRS and DOL ceilings. Everything runs in your browser.
